content.text:
Found the cause. Two facts first:

1. **Your keyring is locked and nothing unlocks it.** `~/.local/share/keyrings/Default_keyring.keyring` is password-protected, there is no `pam_gnome_keyring` in any `/etc/pam.d/*` stack, so every libsecret client triggers a `gcr-prompter` popup. Journal shows dozens today, all cancelled.
2. **TPM won't help you.** You aren't in the `tss` group (`/dev/tpmrm0` is `root:tss 0660`, unreadable), and more importantly a TPM-sealed passphrase unseals for *anything running as you* — same threat model as no password at all. Your home is already homed/LUKS-encrypted, so TPM adds ~nothing on top. `ssh-tpm-agent.service` isn't even loaded right now.

**The better lever:** homed already makes you type your password at tty login. `pam_gnome_keyring.so` is installed at `/usr/lib/security/`. Wire it in and the keyring unlocks with the password you already type — zero popups, keyring stays genuinely encrypted at rest.

Side finding: your systemd `--user` manager is poisoned again this boot (`UnitPath=/.config/systemd/user`), so HM's `gnome-keyring.service` and `ssh-tpm-agent.service` are invisible; Arch's packaged unit is serving secrets instead. Separate issue — flagging it, not fixing it here.

questions.question: How should the keyring get unlocked?

options.label: pam_gnome_keyring (Recommended)
options.description: Add auth+session pam_gnome_keyring.so to the login PAM stack, rename the keyring to `login`, set its password to your login password. Keyring stays encrypted; unlocks silently at tty login. Requires editing a pacman-managed /etc/pam.d file and disabling Arch's gnome-keyring-daemon.socket so PAM's auto_start owns the daemon. ~30 min.

options.label: Empty keyring password
options.description: Strip the password off Default_keyring so gnome-keyring auto-unlocks it. Secrets then protected only by FDE + file perms — the exact model you already accepted for pass-secret-service on fujiwara. ~5 min, no system files touched.

options.label: TPM-sealed passphrase anyway
options.description: Add yourself to `tss` via homectl, seal a random passphrase with systemd-creds --with-key=tpm2, unseal it from a user unit and pipe to `gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock`. Most work, and buys little over FDE — but keeps the keyring file useless off this machine.

set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops

if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2

# so both the config and the token must reach the daemon at the system level.

# The token is sops-encrypted in ../secrets.yaml: decrypt as the user (GCP KMS),

if ! sudo grep -qF 'nix.custom.conf' /etc/nix/nix.conf 2>/dev/null; then
  echo '!include nix.custom.conf' | sudo tee -a /etc/nix/nix.conf >/dev/null

  # The login collection can only be unlocked *at daemon startup*: running

  # and PAM's `--login` both work). So this wrapper *is* the daemon -- it unseals
  # the passphrase and hands it to gnome-keyring-daemon on stdin.
  #
  # The passphrase is 32 random bytes sealed to the TPM's owner hierarchy. Only
  # seal.pub/seal.priv are kept; the parent is re-derived from a fixed template
  # on every start, so there is no persistent handle to allocate or clean up.
  # Threat model: any process running as this user can unseal it, exactly like
  # a passphraseless keyring. What it buys over an empty passphrase is that the
  # keyring file is useless off this machine -- nothing more. Prompts stop
  # either way; this is the cheaper-to-lose-a-laptop version.

  # deliberately NOT wired into sops.secrets: if it were, sops-nix would decrypt

  # storage for re-sealing only (see gnome-keyring-tpm-seal below).

    set -uo pipefail

    # The nixpkgs tpm2-tools build defaults to tcti-abrmd, a resource-manager
    # daemon this host does not run; talk to the kernel RM device instead.
    # Reading it needs the `tss` group (granted in system/deploy).
    export TPM2TOOLS_TCTI="device:/dev/tpmrm0"

    RUN="''${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/run/user/$(id -u)}"

    # Service at all. Both fallbacks log loudly: the symptom is the unlock popup
